claim: Neurexin1α knockout mice exhibited reduced selection of beneficial outcomes in value-based choice paradigms.
source: We found Neurexin1α knockouts exhibited reduced selection of beneficial outcomes and impaired avoidance of costlier options.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Neurexin1α knockout mice exhibited impaired avoidance of costlier options in value-based choice paradigms.
source: We found Neurexin1α knockouts exhibited reduced selection of beneficial outcomes and impaired avoidance of costlier options.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Choice abnormalities in Neurexin1α knockout mice are driven by deficits in updating and representation of value.
source: Reinforcement modeling suggested that this was driven by deficits in updating and representation of value.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract based on reinforcement modeling results.

claim: Disruption of Neurexin1α within telencephalic excitatory projection neurons recapitulated choice abnormalities of global Neurexin1α knockouts.
source: Disruption of Neurexin1α within telencephalic excitatory projection neurons, but not thalamic neurons, recapitulated choice abnormalities of global Neurexin1α knockouts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from region-specific deletion experiments.

claim: Disruption of Neurexin1α within thalamic neurons did not recapitulate choice abnormalities of global Neurexin1α knockouts.
source: Disruption of Neurexin1α within telencephalic excitatory projection neurons, but not thalamic neurons, recapitulated choice abnormalities of global Neurexin1α knockouts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from region-specific deletion experiments.

claim: Selective forebrain excitatory knockout of Neurexin1α perturbed value-modulated neural signals within striatum.
source: Furthermore, this selective forebrain excitatory knockout of Neurexin1α perturbed value-modulated neural signals within striatum, a central node in feedback-based reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract based on neural recording data.

claim: Striatum is a central node in feedback-based reinforcement learning.
source: Furthermore, this selective forebrain excitatory knockout of Neurexin1α perturbed value-modulated neural signals within striatum, a central node in feedback-based reinforcement learning.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Goal-directed behaviors are essential for normal function.
source: Goal-directed behaviors are essential for normal function and significantly impaired in neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: Goal-directed behaviors are significantly impaired in neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Goal-directed behaviors are essential for normal function and significantly impaired in neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge.

claim: Molecular contributions to goal-directed dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders remain unclear despite extensive genetic associations.
source: Despite extensive associations between genetic mutations and these disorders, the molecular contributions to goal-directed dysfunction remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: Cortical regions including orbital frontal cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex represent aspects of reward value and history.
source: Cortical regions including orbital frontal (OFC), medial prefrontal (mPFC), and anterior cingulate (ACC) represent aspects of reward value and history (Bari et al., 2019; Bartra et al., 2013; Euston et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2011; Padoa-Schioppa and Conen, 2017; Rushworth et al., 2011; Rushworth et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: Primary sensory cortices represent reward-associated environmental signals.
source: Primary sensory cortices and midline thalamic nuclei represent reward-associated environmental signals (Parker et al., 2019; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Midline thalamic nuclei represent reward-associated environmental signals.
source: Primary sensory cortices and midline thalamic nuclei represent reward-associated environmental signals (Parker et al., 2019; Znamenskiy and Zador, 2013)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Motor thalamic nuclei ensure smooth performance of actions.
source: while motor thalamic nuclei ensure smooth performance of actions (Díaz-Hernández et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Flexible adaptation of value signals is supported by error-monitoring signals within anterior cingulate cortex and basolateral amygdala.
source: Furthermore, flexible adaptation of value signals is supported by error-monitoring signals within ACC and basolateral amygdala, as well as reward prediction errors encoded by striatal-targeting midbrain dopaminergic neurons (McGuire et al., 2014; Schultz et al., 1997; Ullsperger et al., 2014; Yacubian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Flexible adaptation of value signals is supported by reward prediction errors encoded by striatal-targeting midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
source: Furthermore, flexible adaptation of value signals is supported by error-monitoring signals within ACC and basolateral amygdala, as well as reward prediction errors encoded by striatal-targeting midbrain dopaminergic neurons (McGuire et al., 2014; Schultz et al., 1997; Ullsperger et al., 2014; Yacubian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The dorsal striatum can simultaneously mediate action selection, motor performance, and reinforcement learning via integration of diverse projections.
source: The dorsal striatum via integration of these diverse projections can simultaneously mediate action selection, motor performance, and reinforcement learning (Balleine et al., 2007; Cox and Witten, 2019; Lee et al., 2015; Vo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Deficits in goal-directed decision making are a core endophenotype shared across neuropsychiatric disorders including schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Tourette syndrome.
source: Deficits in goal-directed decision making, and specifically in how reward shapes selection of actions, are a core endophenotype shared across neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders (ASD), obsessive-compulsive disorder, and Tourette syndrome (Barch and Dowd, 2010; Corbett et al., 2009; Dichter et al., 2012; Dowd et al., 2016; Gillan and Robbins, 2014; Griffiths et al., 2014; Hill, 2004; Maia and Frank, 2011; Solomon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: In schizophrenia, impairments in action-outcome learning may reflect perturbations to reinforcement learning error signals or the manner in which they are integrated to impact choice.
source: In schizophrenia, impairments in action–outcome learning (Gold et al., 2015; Morris et al., 2015) may reflect perturbations to reinforcement learning error signals or the manner in which they are integrated to impact choice (Hernaus et al., 2019; Hernaus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Autism spectrum disorder patients exhibit reinforcement learning deficits with impaired choice accuracy driven by reduced win-stay choice patterns.
source: Recent studies have also revealed reinforcement learning deficits in ASD patients (Hill, 2004; Solomon et al., 2015), with impaired choice accuracy driven by reduced win–stay choice patterns (Solomon et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Genetic association studies for neuropsychiatric disease have converged on synapses as key sites of disease pathophysiology.
source: Genetic association studies for neuropsychiatric disease have converged on synapses as key sites of disease pathophysiology (DDD Study et al., 2014; Willsey et al., 2013; Willsey and State, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Rare de novo and inherited copy number variants in Neurexin1α confer significant risk for autism spectrum disorders, schizophrenia, Tourette syndrome, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
source: Neurexin1α (Nrxn1α) is an evolutionarily conserved synaptic adhesion molecule, for which rare de novo and inherited copy number variants confer significant risk for ASDs, schizophrenia, Tourette syndrome, and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Ching et al., 2010; Duong et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2017; Kirov et al., 2009; Lowther et al., 2017; Rujescu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Neurexin1α is an evolutionarily conserved synaptic adhesion molecule.
source: Neurexin1α (Nrxn1α) is an evolutionarily conserved synaptic adhesion molecule, for which rare de novo and inherited copy number variants confer significant risk for ASDs, schizophrenia, Tourette syndrome, and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Ching et al., 2010; Duong et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2017; Kirov et al., 2009; Lowther et al., 2017; Rujescu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: The Neurexin family of proteins functions as a presynaptic hub for transynaptic binding of numerous postsynaptic partners at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses.
source: The Neurexin family of proteins functions as a presynaptic hub for transynaptic binding of numerous postsynaptic partners at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses (Missler et al., 2003; Südhof, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Neurexins are expressed prior to synaptogenesis.
source: Consistent with their expression prior to synaptogenesis (Harkin et al., 2017; Puschel and Betz, 1995), Neurexins have been implicated in the initial specification and long-term integrity of synapses (Anderson et al., 2015; Aoto et al., 2013; Chubykin et al., 2007; Krueger et al., 2012; Soler-Llavina et al., 2011; Südhof, 2017; Varoqueaux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Neurexins have been implicated in the initial specification and long-term integrity of synapses.
source: Consistent with their expression prior to synaptogenesis (Harkin et al., 2017; Puschel and Betz, 1995), Neurexins have been implicated in the initial specification and long-term integrity of synapses (Anderson et al., 2015; Aoto et al., 2013; Chubykin et al., 2007; Krueger et al., 2012; Soler-Llavina et al., 2011; Südhof, 2017; Varoqueaux et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Nrxn1α transcripts are broadly expressed throughout the brain.
source: While Nrxn1α transcripts are broadly expressed throughout the brain, they are particularly enriched in cortico-striatal-thalamic loops proposed to govern motor control, action selection, and reinforcement learning (Fuccillo et al., 2015; Ullrich et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Nrxn1α transcripts are particularly enriched in cortico-striatal-thalamic loops proposed to govern motor control, action selection, and reinforcement learning.
source: While Nrxn1α transcripts are broadly expressed throughout the brain, they are particularly enriched in cortico-striatal-thalamic loops proposed to govern motor control, action selection, and reinforcement learning (Fuccillo et al., 2015; Ullrich et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include reduced nest building and social memory.
source: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include reduced nest building and social memory, increased aggression and grooming, enhanced rotarod learning, and male-specific reductions in operant responding under increasing variable interval responding schedules (Dachtler et al., 2015; Esclassan et al., 2015; Etherton et al., 2009; Grayton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include increased aggression and grooming.
source: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include reduced nest building and social memory, increased aggression and grooming, enhanced rotarod learning, and male-specific reductions in operant responding under increasing variable interval responding schedules (Dachtler et al., 2015; Esclassan et al., 2015; Etherton et al., 2009; Grayton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include enhanced rotarod learning.
source: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include reduced nest building and social memory, increased aggression and grooming, enhanced rotarod learning, and male-specific reductions in operant responding under increasing variable interval responding schedules (Dachtler et al., 2015; Esclassan et al., 2015; Etherton et al., 2009; Grayton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include male-specific reductions in operant responding under increasing variable interval responding schedules.
source: Behavioral abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout animals include reduced nest building and social memory, increased aggression and grooming, enhanced rotarod learning, and male-specific reductions in operant responding under increasing variable interval responding schedules (Dachtler et al., 2015; Esclassan et al., 2015; Etherton et al., 2009; Grayton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice can perform basic light-guided operant responding with consistent task engagement.
source: We found that Nrxn1α knockout (KO) mice could perform basic light-guided operant responding with consistent task engagement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: Performance in the value-based task was significantly altered by the relative magnitude of rewarded outcomes for both wild-type and knockout animals.
source: Performance in this task was significantly altered by the relative magnitude of rewarded outcomes for both wild-type and KO animals with larger reward contrasts driving more biased choice patterns (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Larger reward contrasts drive more biased choice patterns in both wild-type and knockout animals.
source: Performance in this task was significantly altered by the relative magnitude of rewarded outcomes for both wild-type and KO animals with larger reward contrasts driving more biased choice patterns (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: A global decrease in session performance across relative reward contrasts was observed in Nrxn1α knockout mice as compared to wild type.
source: Nonetheless, we observed a global decrease in session performance across relative reward contrasts in Nrxn1α KO mice as compared to wild type (Figure 1B), without genotypic differences in total reward consumed or task engagement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: There were no genotypic differences in total reward consumed between wild-type and Nrxn1α knockout mice.
source: Nonetheless, we observed a global decrease in session performance across relative reward contrasts in Nrxn1α KO mice as compared to wild type (Figure 1B), without genotypic differences in total reward consumed or task engagement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: There were no genotypic differences in task engagement between wild-type and Nrxn1α knockout mice.
source: Nonetheless, we observed a global decrease in session performance across relative reward contrasts in Nrxn1α KO mice as compared to wild type (Figure 1B), without genotypic differences in total reward consumed or task engagement (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: For both wild-type and knockout animals, the relative magnitude of rewarded outcome has a significant effect on the stay-probability for that alternative.
source: For both WT and KO animals, the relative magnitude of rewarded outcome has a significant effect on the stay-probability for that alternative.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 1C and D.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice exhibit smaller gaps between large reward-stay and small reward-stay behavior compared to wild types.
source: We noted smaller gaps between large reward-stay and small reward-stay behavior in Nrxn1α KOs as compared with wild types (Figure 1C and D), leading to smaller RRS values across reward contrasts and feedback environment (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice have smaller relative reward-stay values across reward contrasts and feedback environments compared to wild types.
source: We noted smaller gaps between large reward-stay and small reward-stay behavior in Nrxn1α KOs as compared with wild types (Figure 1C and D), leading to smaller RRS values across reward contrasts and feedback environment (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: There is a significant correlation between relative reward-stay and performance across genotypes.
source: The significant correlation between RRS and performance across genotypes highlights the importance of outcome sensitivity on task performance (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: No statistically significant alteration in adaptability at contingency switches was noted in Nrxn1α knockout mice.
source: As deficits in behavioral adaptability have been observed across neuropsychiatric disorders and impact performance in this task (Alabi et al., 2019), we compared choice patterns at un-signaled contingency switches, noting no statistically significant alteration in KO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: No performance differences between genotypes were observed in extra-dimensional set-shifting tasks.
source: We further probed cognitive flexibility with extra-dimensional set-shifting and spatial reversal tasks, again observing no performance differences between genotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: No performance differences between genotypes were observed in spatial reversal tasks.
source: We further probed cognitive flexibility with extra-dimensional set-shifting and spatial reversal tasks, again observing no performance differences between genotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1J and K).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: Choice abnormalities in Nrxn1α knockout mice arise from decreased sensitivity to beneficial outcomes as opposed to altered feedback integration or impaired cognitive flexibility.
source: In sum, choice abnormalities in Nrxn1α KO mice arise from decreased sensitivity to beneficial outcomes as opposed to altered feedback integration or impaired cognitive flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion in the results section.

claim: No significant discrepancies in latency to initiate were observed between Nrxn1α wild-type and knockout mice across varied reward environments.
source: We observed no significant discrepancies in latency to initiate between Nrxn1α wild-type and KO mice across varied reward environments (Figure 2A), suggesting that observed outcome-associated choice is not attributable to global task disengagement.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: The relative latency to initiate trials in wild-type animals was significantly modulated by the relative reward ratio.
source: Interestingly, the relative latency to initiate trials in wild-type animals was significantly modulated by the relative reward ratio (Figure 2C, gray), with animals initiating trials more quickly after large reward outcomes than small reward outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Wild-type animals initiate trials more quickly after large reward outcomes than small reward outcomes.
source: Interestingly, the relative latency to initiate trials in wild-type animals was significantly modulated by the relative reward ratio (Figure 2C, gray), with animals initiating trials more quickly after large reward outcomes than small reward outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice were entirely unable to modulate initiation latency in response to the magnitude of previous reward.
source: In contrast, Nrxn1α knockout mice were entirely unable to modulate initiation latency in response to the magnitude of previous reward (Figure 2C, blue).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: The strong inverse correlation between relative reward-stay and initiation latency was lost in Nrxn1α knockout mice.
source: The strong inverse correlation between relative reward-stay and initiation latency was lost in Nrxn1α KO mice (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Nrxn1α mutations disrupt outcome-modulated task engagement.
source: Thus, while there is no difference in average task latencies between wild types and KOs, Nrxn1α mutations disrupt outcome-modulated task engagement.

claim: A fixed elongation of choice latency was observed in Nrxn1α mutants across reward environments.
source: We also observed a fixed elongation of choice latency in Nrxn1α mutants across reward environments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice do not select low-effort alternatives as frequently as wild-type littermates in the effort-based task.
source: Interestingly, Nrxn1α KO mice do not select low-effort alternatives as frequently as wild-type littermates, both during sampling and steady-state periods (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: No significant difference in steady-state task engagement was seen between wild-type and Nrxn1α knockout mice in the effort-based task.
source: While we noted the KOs slowed more over the session (Figure 3B), no significant difference in steady-state task engagement was seen (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: An effect of genotype on choice latency was observed in the effort-based task.
source: We continued to observe an effect of genotype on choice latency (Figure 3D) as in prior tasks.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Wild-type mice and Nrxn1α knockouts heavily discount all but the immediately preceding trial in their choice behavior.
source: We found that wild-type mice and Nrxn1α KOs heavily discount all but the immediately preceding trial (t−1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H), suggesting a significant portion of choice variability can be accounted for by analyzing influences of the t−1 trial.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data from logistic regression analysis.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice exhibit a deficit in the learning rate parameter (α) compared to wild-type controls.
source: Fitting choice data for wild-type and KO mice, we demonstrated that Nrxn1α KO mice have significantly lower α and γ parameters (Figure 4C and D), suggesting a global deficit in the updating and representation of choice values guiding decisions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data from reinforcement modeling.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice exhibit a deficit in the reward compression parameter (γ) compared to wild-type controls.
source: Fitting choice data for wild-type and KO mice, we demonstrated that Nrxn1α KO mice have significantly lower α and γ parameters (Figure 4C and D), suggesting a global deficit in the updating and representation of choice values guiding decisions (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data from reinforcement modeling.

claim: Nrxn1α knockout mice exhibit an enrichment of low ΔQ-value trials.
source: Fitting choice data for wild-type and KO mice, we demonstrated that Nrxn1α KO mice have significantly lower α and γ parameters (Figure 4C and D), suggesting a global deficit in the updating and representation of choice values guiding decisions (Figure 4E).

claim: Cre-mediated recombination in Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ mice results in reduced expression of Nrxn1α mRNA detected by exon 9 probe.
source: mRNA from cortical dissection of Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ revealed a 3.5× decrease in Nrxn1α transcripts spanning exon 9 as compared to Nrxn1αfl/fl; Nex+/+ (Figure 5C, left), and a modest degree of nonsense-mediated decay with a downstream probe (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to RT-qPCR data shown in the figure.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination in Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ mice results in a modest degree of nonsense-mediated decay.
source: mRNA from cortical dissection of Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ revealed a 3.5× decrease in Nrxn1α transcripts spanning exon 9 as compared to Nrxn1αfl/fl; Nex+/+ (Figure 5C, left), and a modest degree of nonsense-mediated decay with a downstream probe (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to RT-qPCR data shown in the figure.

claim: A significant effect of NexCre deletion of Nrxn1α on relative reward stay was observed compared to both control groups.
source: We observed a significant effect of NexCre deletion of Nrxn1α on relative reward stay as compared to both control groups (Figure 5D).

claim: Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ mutant animals were less able to bias their choice patterns toward more beneficial outcomes.

claim: No consistent difference in behavioral flexibility was noted in Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ mice.

source: To test whether deficits in working memory could contribute to our choice phenotype, we assessed spontaneous alternation behavior of Nrxn1αfl/fl; NexCre/+ and Nrxn1αfl/fl; Nex+/+ conditional control littermates, observing no genotypic differences (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).

claim: A significant effect of genotype on reward discrimination parameters was observed in forebrain-specific Nrxn1α knockouts.

claim: Thalamic conditional knockout of Nrxn1α could not recapitulate the deficits in value processing observed in whole-brain Nrxn1α mutants.

claim: There were no significant genotypic differences in any parameters of the fitted reinforcement model in thalamic Nrxn1α conditional knockouts.

claim: No significant genotypic differences in choice allocation away from effortful alternatives were noted in thalamic Nrxn1α conditional knockouts.
source: Additionally, we noted no significant genotypic differences in choice allocation away from effortful alternatives (Figure 6K–M and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons exhibited reproducible Ca2+ activity patterns in relation to trial start, self-initiation, and choice/reward delivery task epochs.
source: Putative direct pathway SPNs (p-dSPNs) exhibited reproducible Ca2+ activity patterns in relation to three task epochs – trial start (center port light on), self-initiation (center port entrance), and choice/reward delivery (side port entry) (Figure 7C), despite exhibiting smaller average signals than during task disengagement (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons exhibited smaller average signals during task engagement than during task disengagement.
source: Putative direct pathway SPNs (p-dSPNs) exhibited reproducible Ca2+ activity patterns in relation to three task epochs – trial start (center port light on), self-initiation (center port entrance), and choice/reward delivery (side port entry) (Figure 7C), despite exhibiting smaller average signals than during task disengagement (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: The lack of similar waveforms on the isosbestic 405 nm channel confirms the specificity of epoch-aligned Ca2+ signals in putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons.
source: The lack of similar waveforms on the isosbestic 405 nm channel confirms the specificity of these epoch-aligned Ca2+ signals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: Most pre-initiation epochs following a 'small reward' trial had elevated activity compared to the population Ca2+ average in wild-type putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons.
source: We found that most pre-initiation epochs following a 'small reward' trial had elevated activity compared to the population Ca2+ average, while trials following 'large reward' had suppressed activity relative to the population average (Figure 7E), a trend similarly present in the population data (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Trials following 'large reward' had suppressed activity relative to the population average in wild-type putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons.
source: We found that most pre-initiation epochs following a 'small reward' trial had elevated activity compared to the population Ca2+ average, while trials following 'large reward' had suppressed activity relative to the population average (Figure 7E), a trend similarly present in the population data (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: For slow ramping in wild-type putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons, (t−1) large reward outcomes result in negative ramping or silencing of activity in comparison with small rewards.
source: We found that both signal components were differentially modulated by reward outcome: (1) for slow ramping, (t−1) large reward outcomes result in negative ramping or silencing of p-dSPN activity in comparison with small rewards (Figure 7G and H); (2) for fast peaking, larger rewards result in steeper peak activity as compared to smaller rewards (Figure 7J and K).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: For fast peaking in wild-type putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons, larger rewards result in steeper peak activity as compared to smaller rewards.
source: We found that both signal components were differentially modulated by reward outcome: (1) for slow ramping, (t−1) large reward outcomes result in negative ramping or silencing of p-dSPN activity in comparison with small rewards (Figure 7G and H); (2) for fast peaking, larger rewards result in steeper peak activity as compared to smaller rewards (Figure 7J and K).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Significant correlations were noted between both slow ramp and fast peak measures and trial-by-trial comparative action values in wild-type putative direct pathway spiny projection neurons.
source: Furthermore, we noted significant correlations between both measures and trial-by-trial comparative action values (Figure 7I and L; see Materials and methods), suggesting these p-dSPN signals may reflect value information employed for future action selection.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Putative direct pathway spiny projection neuron signals may reflect value information employed for future action selection.
source: Furthermore, we noted significant correlations between both measures and trial-by-trial comparative action values (Figure 7I and L; see Materials and methods), suggesting these p-dSPN signals may reflect value information employed for future action selection.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the results section.

claim: No difference was found for the slow ramp signal component between Nex-Control and Nex-Nrxn1αcKO genotypes.
source: While we did not uncover a difference for the slow ramp signal component between genotypes (Figure 8A–C), we found that the slope of the fast peak was consistently lower in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: The slope of the fast peak was consistently lower in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO compared to controls.
source: While we did not uncover a difference for the slow ramp signal component between genotypes (Figure 8A–C), we found that the slope of the fast peak was consistently lower in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: The deficit in fast peak slope in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO was specifically associated with failure to increase peak activity in response to large reward volumes.
source: Furthermore, this deficit was specifically associated with failure to increase peak activity in response to large reward volumes (Figure 8F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: No difference in the frequency or amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents was noted according to retroAAV2.EF1α−3xFLAG-Cre versus retroAAV2.hSyn-GFP-ΔCre virus in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mice.
source: To assure that our strategy for labeling d-SPNs, wherein Cre becomes expressed in the recorded spiny neurons, did not alter recurrent inhibition, we compared a separate set of Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mice injected with either retroAAV2.EF1α−3xFLAG-Cre or retroAAV2.hSyn-GFP-ΔCre (an enzymatically inactive truncated version of Cre) in the SNr and noted no difference in the frequency or amplitude of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) according to virus (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: No difference in miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents was noted in retrograde Cre versus ΔCre viruses in Nrxn1αfl/fl mice.
source: To rule-out any potential effects on excitatory striatal afferents, we performed a similar experiment on Nrxn1αfl/fl mice, again noting no difference in the miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) in retrograde Cre versus ΔCre viruses (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to supplementary figure data.

claim: Telencephalic excitatory neuron-specific Nrxn1α mutants do not exhibit global disruptions of striatal circuit dynamics, but a specific outcome-associated perturbation in fast peak activity prior to trial initiation.
source: Together, these data suggest that telencephalic excitatory neuron-specific Nrxn1α mutants do not exhibit global disruptions of striatal circuit dynamics, but a specific outcome-associated perturbation in fast peak activity prior to trial initiation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section.

claim: Blunting of fast peak dynamics in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mutants was specific to aspects of reward processing.
source: We found that blunting of fast peak dynamics in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mutants was specific to aspects of reward processing – that is, while peak slopes had significant correlation to reward history, reward prediction error, and comparative choice values in wild-type mice, these outcome-sensitive signal components were absent in mutant striatal population dynamics (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data from linear mixed-effects modeling.

claim: Peak slopes had significant correlation to reward history, reward prediction error, and comparative choice values in wild-type mice.
source: We found that blunting of fast peak dynamics in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mutants was specific to aspects of reward processing – that is, while peak slopes had significant correlation to reward history, reward prediction error, and comparative choice values in wild-type mice, these outcome-sensitive signal components were absent in mutant striatal population dynamics (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Outcome-sensitive signal components were absent in mutant striatal population dynamics in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mice.
source: We found that blunting of fast peak dynamics in Nex-Nrxn1αcKO mutants was specific to aspects of reward processing – that is, while peak slopes had significant correlation to reward history, reward prediction error, and comparative choice values in wild-type mice, these outcome-sensitive signal components were absent in mutant striatal population dynamics (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Value-modulated signal components are preserved in the mutants during slow ramping.
source: In contrast, value-modulated signal components are preserved in the mutants during slow ramping (Figure 8H), supporting a circumscribed alteration in striatal value coding.
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to figure data.

claim: Disrupted reward responsive activity in direct pathway spiny projection neurons occurs upon ablation of Nrxn1α in a subset of excitatory forebrain neurons.
source: Together, these data demonstrate disrupted reward responsive activity in direct pathway SPNs upon ablation of Nrxn1α in a subset of excitatory forebrain neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the results section.

claim: Changes in striatal neural signals in Nrxn1α mutants are broadly consistent with behavioral analysis showing lower learning rate and sensitivity to outcome magnitudes.
source: These changes are broadly consistent with our behavioral analysis showing Nrxn1α knockout in frontal projection neurons produced lower learning rate and sensitivity to outcome magnitudes (Figure 5E and F), generating smaller Q value discrepancies (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation in the results section.
